name.text: L2 Q1 Image and running machine

questiontext.text: What is the relationship between a machine image and a virtual machine?

generalfeedback.text: An image provides the starting state for multiple instances. The instances can change independently after launch; those changes do not automatically rewrite the image.

answer.text: The image is the live machine's current CPU and memory usage.
One image can initialize multiple VM instances, which can later develop different state.
Every image can initialize only one VM.
Launching a VM automatically updates the source image whenever the VM changes.

name.text: L2 Q2 Image building and deployment

questiontext.text: What distinguishes building a machine image from deploying machines based on that image?

generalfeedback.text: Image building prepares a reusable artifact. Deployment uses that artifact to create running instances. Producing a new image does not automatically update existing machines or eliminate instance-specific initialization.

answer.text: Building an image automatically replaces every running machine.
Deployment modifies the shared source image whenever an instance changes.
Building an image removes the need for any instance-specific configuration.
Building creates a reusable starting artifact; deployment creates running instances from it.

questiontext.text: The lecture describes a problematic form of a "golden image." What makes that example an anti-pattern?

generalfeedback.text: The problem is hidden manual changes and the lack of a maintained, repeatable creation process. A shared baseline or an automated, rebuildable image is not inherently an anti-pattern, even if the team calls it a golden image.

answer.text: The image was modified manually and cannot be reliably recreated from a maintained build definition.
The organization uses a shared base image.
The image has been tested before use.
The image is generated by an automated build pipeline.

questiontext.text: A team wants to use the same machine baseline on two virtualization platforms and on different processor architectures. Which assumption is sound?

generalfeedback.text: Machine images must be compatible with the destination platform and processor architecture. A common intended baseline can require different artifacts or formats for different targets; the exact requirements depend on the target platforms.

answer.text: Any machine image can boot unchanged on every platform and processor architecture.
Matching the application's name guarantees that its machine image is compatible.
The team must check platform and architecture compatibility and may need separate image variants.
Only disk size determines whether the image can boot.

name.text: L2 Q5 Stock and custom images

questiontext.text: An organization starts every server from a supplied stock image and repeats the same security and software setup at launch. What is the strongest reason to maintain a custom image?

generalfeedback.text: A stock image is a supplied starting point. A custom image adds selected software and configuration, providing a tested baseline and reducing repeated initialization. It still requires maintenance, instance-specific settings, and separate protection of persistent data.

answer.text: A custom image captures live application data, so it replaces the need for separate data backups.
A custom image contains a tested organizational baseline, reducing repeated setup while still requiring maintenance.
A custom image incorporates future security fixes automatically, so its original build definition can remain unchanged.
A custom image removes environment differences, so all settings and machine identities should be embedded in it.

name.text: L2 Q6 Build time and boot time

questiontext.text: A fleet needs the same monitoring software on every machine, but each instance needs a distinct identity and environment-specific connection settings. Which division of work best fits image building and first-start initialization?

generalfeedback.text: Build-time work becomes part of a reusable image; first-start initialization can supply values specific to an instance or environment. Other divisions may be valid, but this one directly separates the stable shared baseline from the varying inputs. First-start initialization alone is not ongoing reconciliation.

answer.text: Embed the monitoring software and one shared machine identity in the image; change environment settings manually after launch.
Install everything at first start because reusable images cannot contain configured software.
Embed all production connection settings in every image; use first-start initialization only to check whether the machine boots.
Prepare the shared monitoring software in the image; supply instance identity and environment settings during first-start initialization.

name.text: L2 Q7 Containers and virtual machines

questiontext.text: Which statement correctly compares a typical Linux container with a virtual machine and identifies a consequence?

generalfeedback.text: Typical Linux containers share a host kernel while isolating aspects of their execution environment. A VM has a guest kernel over virtualized hardware. Kernel sharing affects compatibility and isolation; neither approach guarantees that arbitrary images work on every platform.

answer.text: Containers normally share the host kernel, while VMs run guest kernels; a workload requiring a different kernel may need a VM.
Containers and VMs each boot their own kernel, so they provide the same kernel isolation boundary.
Containers share the host kernel, so they cannot isolate processes or files from other containers.
VMs run guest kernels, so any VM image can run unchanged on every processor architecture and hypervisor.

name.text: L2 Q8 Snapshot and rebuildable definition

questiontext.text: A team has a snapshot of a working server but no maintained definition of how it was configured. Which assessment is most accurate?

generalfeedback.text: A snapshot captures state at a point in time, within its scope and consistency limits. It can support restoration but does not explain the intended build process or make hidden manual changes reviewable. Rebuildable definitions and data backups serve different purposes.

answer.text: The snapshot records the intended configuration process, so future changes can be reviewed directly from its creation history.
The snapshot is unsuitable for recovery because only a rebuildable definition can restore a machine's state.
The snapshot may restore captured state, but a maintained definition is still needed to review and deliberately reproduce the configuration process.
The snapshot proves future builds will match the server, provided the same stock image name is selected each time.

name.text: L2 Q9 Organizing an image family

questiontext.text: Web-server and database-server images share a security baseline but need different software. Their separate build definitions contain copied baseline steps, and a policy update reached only one copy. Which plan best addresses both organization and rollout?

generalfeedback.text: A shared baseline reduces inconsistent copies while workload-specific definitions preserve useful differences. Updating source does not update existing artifacts or instances: affected images must be rebuilt, tested, and deliberately rolled out. Validation should cover both the policy and the workloads.

answer.text: Build one image with both workloads installed; apply a baseline change to whichever running servers currently need it.
Reuse a common baseline with separate workload definitions; rebuild affected images, validate policy and workload behavior, then deliberately replace affected machines.
Reuse a common baseline with separate workload definitions; committing its new version also updates existing images and running machines.
Keep the copied baseline steps and review each copy; validate only the baseline definition before replacing machines with existing images.

name.text: L2 Q10 Reproducible builds and immutable updates

questiontext.text: A version-controlled image build always selects the latest base image and packages. The team wants to reproduce an approved version and later roll out a deliberately patched version. Which plan meets both goals?

generalfeedback.text: Version-controlled instructions do not freeze external inputs such as base images and packages. Reproduction requires controlled versions and available artifacts. An immutable update builds and validates a new image, replaces instances deliberately, and protects persistent data through suitable storage or a verified migration/recovery process.

answer.text: Re-run the same source revision with latest inputs; update existing servers in place and call the unchanged source an immutable release.
Record the approved base image but continue selecting latest packages; replace all machines and recreate their application data from the build definition.
Control both base and package versions; patch running machines manually and rely on their original image for future replacements.
Record and retain approved base and package artifacts; build and validate a patched image, check replacement instances, and preserve persistent data during rollout.
